item.title: Steer Unified Audio Editing Toward Reliable Source Selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.10630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unified audio editors support diverse operations, yet often struggle to modify the intended source while preserving non-target content. We show that source selection in audio editing is shaped by early denoising states, while incorrect early selections can hardly be corrected during subsequent denoising. Motivated by these findings, we propose Source-selection Training via Early-trajectory Emphasis and Recovery (STEER), a two-stage post-training algorithm for reliable selective audio editing. STEER-Emphasis prioritizes training on task-critical early states to reduce source-selection errors, while STEER-Recovery learns corrective denoising from self-generated rollout states to recover from early deviations. To systematically assess source-selection reliability, we introduce the Selective Audio Editing Benchmark, enabling large-scale automatic evaluation of target manipulation and non-target preservation. Applying STEER to our pretrained multitask base editor gives SteerSound, a unified audio editor with leading selective editing performance among open-source audio editors. Experiments on our base editor, UNISON, and SAM Audio demonstrate that STEER consistently improves both selective editing capability and overall editing performance. Early-trajectory emphasis further brings substantial improvements in transcript-conditioned target speaker removal and separation, highlighting the broader applicability of this training principle.
item.dc:creator: Youquan Fu, Dongnuan Cai, Yu Pan, Henghui Du, Yujia Zhang, Ping Luo, Quande Liu, Yake Wei, Xi Chen, Hongyuan Zhang, Di Hu

item.title: Machine Hearing: Can Audio LLMs Generalize Beyond Human Auditory Perception?
item.description: arXiv:2611.10693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal LLMs have made remarkable progress in perceiving the physical world, while their perceptual scope remains largely human-centric, focusing on what humans can directly see or hear. This progress raises the prospect of perception beyond human limits, such as extending hearing to sounds that are inaudible to humans. More broadly, the physical world is full of waves, vibrations, and oscillations, only a small fraction of which are directly audible to humans. This invites the extension of multimodal LLMs toward a broader form of machine hearing, which remains largely underexplored. To investigate this direction, we introduce the Machine Hearing Benchmark (MHB), comprising 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains. MHB spans highly heterogeneous input regimes, with sampling rates from approximately $10^{-5}$ to $10^6$ Hz, sequence lengths from $10^1$ to $10^6$ samples, and both single- and multi-channel inputs. Evaluations of current open-source and proprietary Audio LLMs (ALLMs) reveal limited zero-shot transfer to machine hearing. Supervised adaptation on machine-hearing data alone does not close this gap, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond data exposure to a systematic mismatch between existing audio front ends and machine-hearing inputs. To address this mismatch, we introduce MachEar, a lightweight encoder extension that complements the pretrained Audio LLM for machine-hearing inputs. The results show that MachEar equips a pretrained Audio LLM with stronger machine-hearing capabilities while largely preserving its existing audio understanding performance.
item.dc:creator: Liwei Liu, Jun Tao, Xingyuan Li, Xuenan Xu, Chen Zhang, Junyi Wang, Boya Zhang, Xiaoyu Yang, Zhen-Hua Ling, Wen Wu, Chao Zhang

item.title: Patchbay: a block model for the sonification of ADS-B aircraft data
item.description: arXiv:2611.10973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Patchbay is a design for turning the data that an ADS-B receiver collects into sound by wiring typed blocks together. ADS-B reports are the position and altitude messages that aircraft broadcast and that a small ground receiver can collect. We first describe what such a receiver reports: signals that differ in shape (continuous, stepped, circular, categorical), in resolution, in who produces them, and in how long they stay put, which runs from about ten seconds to the whole time an aircraft is in view. From this we derive a small model. Four kinds of connection carry an aircraft set, a value, an event or audio, and 27 blocks select aircraft, read fields, decide when a note starts, shape values and make sound. One of these blocks makes the receiver act as a radar: scanning by bearing it is a line that rotates about the receiver, and scanning by range it is a ring that grows from the centre or shrinks inward. Each aircraft sounds at the moment the scan reaches it, and the scan's period is set in bars of a beat clock. The model does not depend on a browser. Our reference implementation is a browser editor, contained in one HTML file, that replays two recorded captures and records both an audio take and a MIDI take, a file of the notes played rather than of the sound. We say what is not built and place the work beside the closest systems we found, among them a radar-sweep sequencer for tangible objects from 2006 and a range-ring sonification of ADS-B aircraft published in 2026. Sweeps that trigger sound, and typed connections, both exist in earlier systems. To our knowledge, none of the sources we reached carries the aircraft in view, with every field attached, as one kind of connection in an editor.
item.dc:creator: Arquimedes Canedo

item.title: GlobalTap: Globally Diverse Beat Tracking Benchmark via Crowdsourced Tapping
item.description: arXiv:2611.11137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing beat-tracking benchmarks draw from a narrow range of musical cultures, predominantly Western, and are difficult to scale due to reliance on expert annotation. We address both limits with GlobalTap, a benchmark of 200 popular-music excerpts spanning 59 countries, annotated by 746 participants recruited across ten countries. The benchmark is created using a scalable online tapping pipeline that records taps via audio for high temporal precision, aggregates pooled tap times into consensus beat annotations, and computes intrinsic quality measures that flag perceptually difficult excerpts without requiring a reference. In a separate study on a different 240-excerpt validation set, tapped by an additional 733 participants, an independent group of 130 listeners rated how well the resulting beat tracks lined up with the music, and we detected no overall difference between our annotations and existing reference annotations. Crowd-derived annotations occasionally diverged from the references in phase and metrical interpretation, yet listeners did not consistently prefer the reference versions, suggesting that crowd-derived and existing reference annotations can reflect different perceptual or structural interpretations. The disagreements were often systematic rather than random, and metrical-level choices differed across the ten recruitment countries. We release GlobalTap together with open-source pipeline code as a listener-derived resource for evaluating beat-tracking systems on culturally diverse music.
item.dc:creator: William T. Botticelli-Wells, Manuel Anglada-Tort, Elif Celen, Rena Far, Harin Lee, Peter M. C. Harrison, Nori Jacoby

item.title: Guidance at Pure Noise Erodes Speaker Similarity in Few-Step Token-Conditioned Flow-Matching TTS
item.description: arXiv:2611.11179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-speech systems built from a language model and a flow-matching mel decoder now run the decoder with two to four Euler steps instead of the official ten or more. At two steps the word error rate (WER) is unchanged, but speaker similarity (SIM) drops by one to six points. This paper shows that most of this loss comes from classifier-free guidance on the first step. At pure noise the network can only return the conditional mean, so guidance shifts every trajectory by nearly the same vector. Later steps do not remove this shift, and its size grows with the length of the first step, so it is negligible with ten or more steps and accounts for most of the loss with two. Two training-free samplers are derived from this analysis. First-step unguided sampling (FSU) leaves the first step unguided and recovers $84$--$91\%$ of the two-step SIM loss on CosyVoice~2/3 with no significant WER increase. FSU-Mid replaces the two Euler steps by one midpoint step with an unguided first evaluation, recovers $77$--$85\%$ on IndexTTS-2 and matches the ten-step teacher on CosyVoice~2 and GLM-TTS. Both use three network function evaluations, one fewer than the official two-step sampler, and FSU-Mid gives the highest mean recovery among eight published guidance rules re-run at two steps on four decoders.
item.dc:creator: Jaeho Lee, Han-Lim Choi

item.title: Real-Time Arbitrary Resampling for Phase-Continuous Microtuning in Audio Streams
item.description: arXiv:2611.11282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops an output-driven resampling formulation for fine pitch adjustment of recorded signals. A fractional input-position increment combines the desired frequency ratio with independently specified input and output sample rates. Each output sample is evaluated from neighboring input samples, and gradual rate changes preserve the current input position. Musical interval mapping and direct sine synthesis are treated as distinct layers. The formulation separates tuning resolution, numerical accuracy, interpolation quality, and streaming correctness. Optional rational-factor representations use freely chosen approximation parameters; numerical illustrations do not define constants required by the algorithm. Linear interpolation provides a low-cost evaluation kernel but does not establish a universal signal-quality or frequency-accuracy guarantee.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Falkenberg

item.title: DIY Customized Speech Recognition for a Person with Speech Disabilities
item.description: arXiv:2611.11327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: General-purpose state-of-the-art automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems fail systematically for speakers with moderate to severe speech disabilities. This paper describes the design, implementation, and evaluation of a customized ASR system built for the first author, a researcher with cerebral palsy and dysarthria. We fine-tuned OpenAI's Whisper medium and large-v3 models using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on audio samples recorded from the first author's own speech on consumer-grade hardware. On a held-out test set of 100 previously unseen utterances, the corresponding transcriptions resulted in a Word Error Rate drop from 49% to 17% for medium and from 30% to 12% for large-v3, while the Character Error Rate fell from 26% to 7% for medium and from 16% to 5% for large-v3, indicating that the residual errors are minor phonemic substitutions. Based on these models, the first author developed AVoz, a mobile application that acts as a real-time interpreter, converting his speech into synthesized voice for the listener. All processing is performed locally, ensuring that no audio data leaves the user's machine. We argue that the methodology is replicable. Moreover, we publish the full LoRA configuration, the implementation, and a step-by-step recording and training protocol, so that other people with speech disabilities, or their family members and caregivers, can build their own systems with a few hours of labeled audio data and a couple of days of GPU time.
item.dc:creator: Paulo A. Condado, Fernando G. Lobo

item.title: Small Data Generative AI for Culturally Specific Artistic Creation: A Case Study on the Sonic Space of sarir
item.description: arXiv:2611.11374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale generative AI (GenAI) models have become increasingly integrated into contemporary creative practice, yet they often reproduce cultural biases and fail to meaningfully engage with non-Western artistic traditions. In response, this paper explores a small-data approach that foregrounds artist-curated and culturally informed dataset creation and model training. Through a case study on sarir (the distinctive sound produced by the reed pen in Persian calligraphy), we demonstrate how small-data GenAI can operate within a highly situated cultural context that lies beyond the representational reach of large-scale GenAI models. We construct a bespoke sarir audio dataset and train two models, RAVE and StyleGAN2, adapting each to the sonic domain through audio synthesis and spectrogram generation. The resulting models learn the fine-grained timbral and gestural nuances of sarir, enabling both real-time interaction and extended generative output. By comparing these results with state-of-the-art text-to-audio models, we clearly demonstrate the disparity in their performance and highlight the expressive possibilities unlocked through the small data approach. This focused case study demonstrates the feasibility of small-data GenAI for culturally specific artistic creation and underscores the value of further investigations that extend this approach to other cultural materials and artistic domains.
item.dc:creator: Arshia Sobhan, Paul Triana, Philippe Pasquier

item.title: When Normality Shifts: Multi-Level WavLM Modeling for Open-World Audio Deepfake Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.11465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio deepfake detectors trained with known synthesis attacks can learn generator-specific shortcuts that fail as synthesis systems and acoustic conditions evolve. We investigate an attack-free alternative: a normality model trained exclusively on bona fide speech, which scores synthetic audio by its deviation from authentic representations. We propose MLN-WavLM, a method that applies shrinkage-Mahalanobis modeling to pooled hidden states from a frozen large-scale, pre-trained speech processing WavLM Base+ architecture. Evaluated on ASVspoof 2019 LA, our best attack-free variant achieves an 8.45\% Equal Error Rate (EER), closely tracking a fully supervised WavLM-HM-Conformer baseline (7.86%). However, when subjected to the ASVspoof 2021 DF domain shift, performance drops to 22.12% EER, exposing vulnerabilities in the bona-fide-calibrated operating point. Layer-wise analysis reveals that early WavLM representations dominate the ensemble. To test real-world viability, we simulated deployment streams using unlabeled threshold adaptation. While robust median/MAD recalibration easily handles in-domain contamination up to 10%, recalibrating under the 2021 DF domain shift triggers a total collapse of low-FPR recall. We conclude that while frozen source-domain normality can effectively rank deepfakes, it does not yield a stable open-world decision rule, and downstream threshold adaptation cannot rescue upstream ranking degradation.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Niekurzak, Daniel Kozuch, Weronika Folwarska, Khan Muhammad, Rafa{\l} Scherer

item.title: Music Inpainting With Similarity-Guided Latent Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2611.11522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a music inpainting technique combining similarity matching and a diffusion-based generative model to replace large segments of audio recordings with suitable alternatives. The proposed hybrid method, Similarity-Guided Diffusion Posterior Sampling (SimDPS), retrieves candidate replacement segments from the wider signal based on contextual similarity and uses them to guide the diffusion process toward coherent reconstructions. Being model-agnostic, the framework is compatible with any pre-trained diffusion model operating in either the waveform or latent domain. Objective evaluations demonstrate that SimDPS outperforms widely adopted RePaint and DPS methods across acoustic features and neural-embedding distance metrics. Subjective evaluations on multi-genre music datasets confirm that SimDPS enhances perceptual plausibility compared to previous diffusion-based methods and demonstrates robustness to poorly matched similarity candidates. These findings pave the way for improved music restoration and context-aware audio editing.
item.dc:creator: Sean Turland, Eloi Moliner, Vesa V\"alim\"aki

item.title: From Sound to Occupancy: Privacy-Aware Audio Sensing for Buildings
item.description: arXiv:2611.11564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Occupancy-based controls regulate lighting and HVAC according to whether a space is in use. Passive infrared (PIR) sensors, the most common choice, respond to motion and can report an occupied room as vacant when its occupants remain still. Sound offers an alternative cue, since seated occupants type, turn pages and cough, but microphones raise privacy concerns. We therefore study a two-stage design: an on-device encoder maps each second of audio to a short embedding, and a server-side temporal model turns the stream of embeddings into an occupancy state. To our knowledge, no publicly available dataset pairs office audio with occupancy labels, so we evaluate the two stages separately on public data. The encoder is trained on synthetic scenes that mix empty-room recordings, room impulse responses, office sounds and read speech, and tested on unseen rooms, recordings and speakers for whether a second contains a sound made by a person. On 11 real office recordings (DCASE 2013) it reaches an AUC of 0.87, against 0.76 for log-mel statistics. Attacks on the transmitted embeddings recover at most 1% of the spoken words, against 94% from log-mel frames, but still identify the speaker among 40 in 69 to 77% of the utterances. Noise-floor normalization with adversarial training, an 8-dimensional embedding, or sending only class probabilities lowers this to 38 to 55% without hurting detection. On HPDmobile, which pairs home occupancy labels with an amplitude envelope of the audio, a causal temporal model pretrained with a hierarchical contrastive loss matches hand-crafted features (AUC 0.75) and does better when only one labelled day per home is available. These results make the two-stage design a practical basis for privacy-aware acoustic occupancy sensing, with speaker identity as the one leak still to close.
item.dc:creator: Myeongwon Chae, Seonghyuk Son

item.title: LAION-Audio-XL: A Web-Scale Corpus and Scaling Studies for Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining
item.description: arXiv:2611.11592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent progress on contrastive audio-language models can be attributed mainly to the scale and quality of their training data. Larger training datasets expose models to a broader range of sounds and corresponding audio captions. To exploit this, we collect 1.48 billion audio samples from academic datasets, internet datasets, web collections, Common Crawl, and YouTube, and process them with a multi-stage curation pipeline. Furthermore, we generate short and long captions for samples in our corpus that lack them. We use our dataset to study the scaling behavior of contrastive audio-language models based on the NaFlex architecture for the audio encoder. Our experiments identify trade-offs between model size and training data for a given compute budget. Moreover, our resulting models, CLAP2, outperform prior audio-text models of comparable size on the MAEB and HEAR benchmarks. We release our dataset, captions, model checkpoints, and code.
item.dc:creator: Gijs Wijngaard, Felix F\"orster, Ross Wightman, Marianna Nezhurina, Christoph Schuhmann, Jenia Jitsev, A. Sophia Koepke

item.title: Towards Trustworthy Mobile Speech Interaction: Ensuring Voice Authenticity and Transmission Integrity
item.description: arXiv:2611.11777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid progress of generative speech models has made high-fidelity voice cloning and editing cheap, fast, and widely accessible, weakening the security of voiceprint-based authentication in mobile speech interactions. Existing speech watermarking techniques focus on offline protection or watermarking synthetic speech, and thus cannot verify whether a live utterance originates from the genuine speaker at capture time. We present \textit{MoBiMark}, a real-time \textbf{mo}bile \textbf{bi}ologic speech water\textbf{mark}ing system that binds ultrasonic articulatory signatures to speech content and embeds a dynamic watermark during capture. MoBiMark emits a multi-frequency ultrasonic probe on commodity smartphones, extracts echo features from the vocal tract, and fuses them with a content-dependent speech embedding to produce a dual-layer dynamic watermark combining a persistent user identifier (UID) and a per-utterance speech identifier (SID), enabling both source authentication and propagation-time tamper detection. A jointly trained embedder and detector injects the watermark while preserving perceptual quality, and system-level optimization with INT8 quantization enables lightweight on-device deployment. Evaluated on 50 users across four smartphone models, MoBiMark achieves an average 99.79% accuracy in source and propagation attacks, with negligible impact on speech quality and intelligibility.
item.dc:creator: Guodong Liu, Lei Wang, Dongxu Liu, Qianran Qiao, Haipeng Dai, He Huang, Guihai Chen

item.title: Reverberant Speech Conditioning for Material-Aware Acoustic Parameter Mapping
item.description: arXiv:2611.11834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dense maps of room acoustic parameters (T30, EDT, C50, DRR) describe how a room sounds at every position. Scene-wide estimation predicts such maps from a floor plan but requires a reference impulse response, which is hard to obtain. Our system instead receives a floor plan and easily recorded reverberant speech from one talker-microphone pair. We compare four speech-derived conditioning inputs: MFCCs, an embedding from the blind estimator BERP, BERP's scalar reverberation-time estimate, and an impulse response reconstructed by Rec-RIR. Our main benchmark is the MRAS dataset, where material assignments vary at fixed geometry. The reconstructed impulse response performs best among the four inputs, reducing T30 error from 31.5% with the floor plan alone to 19.9%, 83% of the reduction achieved by the reference response. We find that adding speech mainly sets the overall level of the map, with little improvement in predicting how the acoustics vary across the room.
item.dc:creator: Yi Wu, Olha Townsend, Qianqian Fang, Magdalena Fuentes, You Zhang

item.title: MUTE: Multi-Level Alignment Uncoupling Against Talking-Head Exploitation for Voice Protection
item.description: arXiv:2611.11989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Talking-head generation models, which synthesize realistic facial animations from audio, are increasingly vulnerable to misuse in multimodal deepfake scenarios. Protecting such systems remains challenging, as talking-head models fundamentally rely on precise audio-visual alignment, while effective audio protection methods remain largely underexplored. In this work, we propose MUTE, an audio protection framework that uncouples the underlying audio-visual alignment through a multi-level strategy. Specifically, MUTE combines (1) Alignment-level Disruption, which directly perturbs cross-modal attention to disrupt structural alignment, and (2) Representation-level Degradation, which perturbs temporal audio embeddings to degrade their representations. To improve robustness, perturbations are constrained in the STFT domain to high-energy regions, making them resistant to post-processing, denoising, and adaptive attacks. An optional speaker-level objective further mitigates potential bypass via TTS-based resynthesis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MUTE consistently degrades lip synchronization across both white-box and black-box talking-head models while preserving perceptual audio quality. The proposed method remains effective under real-world transformations and can be combined with image-based approaches to provide stronger multimodal protection. The source code and project page are available at https://github.com/jindl465/MUTE.
item.dc:creator: Donghyun Kim, Jin Hong, Seungmin Kim, Dain Kim, Junseok Kwon, Daeseon Choi

item.title: Constraining Evidence Strength in Bayesian Tonal-State Inference: A Posterior-Continuity Diagnostic
item.description: arXiv:2611.12006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective pitch-evidence strength governs the concentration of tonal-state posteriors. Expert local-key annotations cannot calibrate this strength because they do not specify the posterior distribution over the 24 candidate keys. This study constrains evidence strength through tonal continuity, quantified by a measure $\lambda$ derived from adjacent-window posterior overlap. Passages with $\lambda$ > 0.50 exhibit relatively strong tonal continuity. At $\lambda$ = 0.50, carrying forward the preceding tonal belief is predictively equivalent to starting afresh with a uniform, key-neutral prior. Across 26 subcorpora of the Distant Listening Corpus, median $\lambda$ remains above 0.50 for changes from major keys to IV, V, and vi throughout the examined range of evidence strengths, whereas changes to i, ii, and iii cross this threshold as evidence strength increases. Because these latter three keys share the departed key's tonic or differ from it by a single key-signature accidental, such changes are expected to retain $\lambda$ > 0.50 in a substantial proportion of cases. An event share G therefore assesses how often this expectation holds as tonal selectivity increases in 4-bar windows. The resulting high-G region identifies evidence-strength settings that may be appropriate for tonal-state inference. When $\lambda$ is extended to cross-scale compatibility, the Presto finale of Mozart's Piano Sonata K. 310 shows that, within this region, a 4-bar C-minor interpretation remains compatible with its 16-bar C-major context. The findings establish tonal continuity as a music-theoretical constraint on evidence strength and illustrate how local and prevailing-key interpretations can coexist when pitch evidence is integrated over nested spans.
item.dc:creator: Chen-Gia Tsai

item.title: BARS: Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis via Flow Matching
item.description: arXiv:2611.12061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present BARS (Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis), a non-autoregressive rapping voice generation model based on Flow Matching, conditioned on a beat track (instrumental backing), lyrics, and a short reference voice for zero-shot timbre control. Unlike prior autoregressive rap synthesis, where rap pace and output duration are strictly determined by the beat, BARS enables independent control over the rap tempo, allowing flexible-length generation without explicit duration prediction or phoneme-level alignment. We encode lyrics using a pretrained ByT5 encoder with a lightweight Transformer adapter trained jointly with the model, without relying on speech-pretrained text encoders, enabling natural handling of non-standard orthography (e.g., slang, abbreviations) and numerals common in rap lyrics. To address alignment instabilities, such as token skipping or repetition, under strong beat conditioning, we propose Asymmetric Scaled RoPE for cross-attention, which introduces a positional structure to facilitate sequential lyric-audio alignment learning. Furthermore, the model supports partial re-generation via span masking, enabling lyric-level editing while preserving the surrounding vocal style. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high lyric fidelity, natural rap flow that is rhythmically coherent with the beat, and robust tempo control across a wide range of rapping styles and speeds.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 27th International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference (ISMIR), 2026
item.dc:creator: Taemin Cho, Hector Martel, Enyan Koh

item.title: AudioCodex: Streaming Autoencoders for Live Audio
item.description: arXiv:2611.12375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce AudioCodex, a fully causal autoencoder for live generative audio applications that compresses stereo audio into compact continuous latent sequences at ~10 Hz. It combines a Mean Flow magnitude autoencoder with latent hypersphere projection, bounded-noise augmentation, representation alignment, and adversarial phase recovery to learn representations that support both efficient downstream generation and high-quality reconstruction. Through extensive ablations, we show that AudioCodex outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of generation-reconstruction trade-off, whilst remaining strictly causal in both encoding and decoding. This work paves the way towards truly real-time interactive and streaming generative audio applications.
item.dc:creator: Marco Pasini, Javier Nistal, Cyran Aouameur, Stefan Lattner, George Fazekas

item.title: Textraction: Unified Text-Guided Speaker Extraction and Enhancement for Single- and Multi-Channel Audio
item.description: arXiv:2611.12493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Textraction, a text-guided speaker extraction framework that enables the selective extraction of desired speakers or noise sources from an audio mixture using only natural-language descriptions. The proposed method operates within a single unified model that supports both single-channel and multi-channel inputs and it allows conditioning on either semantic textual descriptions of the target source or on its spatial description. Dedicated single- and multi-channel encoders feed a shared stack of time--frequency transformer blocks, which is conditioned on the prompt and on the recording configuration in every block through cross-attention and estimates the target directly from the mixture in one forward pass, without a separation stage or a source-selection stage. The system can extract an arbitrary subset of entities from a mixture, assuming up to two simultaneously active speakers and two noise sources, and interprets prompts specifying which entities to keep, which to remove, or both. In addition, we show that the framework naturally applies to a speech-enhancement setting, in which a single target speaker is present alongside background noise. To circumvent the application of computationally costly large language models used in prior work, we introduce a lightweight, task-adapted text encoder obtained by contrastively fine-tuning a compact text-retrieval model, which learns to be sensitive to instruction polarity (e.g., keep vs. remove) while remaining robust to paraphrasing. Experiments across attribute-based extraction, spatially guided extraction, and speech enhancement show that the proposed approach effectively isolates the desired entities under various acoustic and spatial conditions, and matches or surpasses dedicated spatial-extraction and enhancement baselines while offering substantially greater flexibility.
item.dc:creator: Aviad Eisenberg, Sharon Gannot, Shlomo E. Chazan

item.title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.12527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work proposes WaveGen, a fully end-to-end diffusion-based text-to-waveform framework based on Spectral Forcing, which jointly learns an internal spectral trajectory and the target waveform trajectory within a single model, enabling direct end-to-end text-to-waveform generation. Unlike recent TTS pipelines, WaveGen does not rely on separately trained or externally decoded intermediate representations, such as neural audio codecs, Mel-spectrogram vocoders, or VAE-based latent models. In addition, WaveGen performs internal text-speech alignment within a single model, eliminating the need for external alignment modules such as duration predictors. To preserve a truly end-to-end formulation, our framework further avoids dependence on self-supervised representations, such as BERT-based text embeddings and Wav2Vec 2.0-based semantic representations, as well as semantic distillation methods for training optimization. To achieve this, we carefully design Spectral Forcing, a model architecture with disentangled diffusion heads, and a training objective based on a multi-scale spectral $v$-loss. We further validate the scalability of end-to-end TTS models by scaling the model size from 0.1B to 0.6B parameters. Using a single architecture, open-source data, and one-stage training, without external modules such as duration predictor or REPA, WaveGen demonstrates fully end-to-end waveform generation achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Emilia training dataset. In particular, WaveGen achieves a WER of 1.47 and a SIM of 0.75 on the Seed-en benchmark. Source code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen
item.dc:creator: Sang-Hoon Lee, Ha-Yeong Choi

item.title: Direct Conditioning of Audio Diffusion Transformers on fMRI Reveals Cortical Contributions to Sound Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.12603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructing audio from brain activity remains challenging. Existing brain-to-audio pipelines typically map neural responses to predefined stimulus representations before synthesis. While recent work in the visual domain has explored direct conditioning on brain activity, this approach has not yet been extended to audio diffusion models. We introduce MAAS (Multi-Area Auditory Synthesis), an end-to-end framework that conditions a pretrained audio diffusion transformer on ROI-wise fMRI responses without first supervising a decoder to predict an external stimulus representation. MAAS uses region-specific projections and learned brain tokens to condition Stable Audio through a dedicated cross-attention pathway. On a 7T fMRI dataset, we demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines, including two-stage fMRI-to-latent conditioning, across both acoustic and semantic evaluation metrics. In addition, we introduce a fidelity metric grounded in a computational model of auditory neural processing, which allows us to quantify the contribution of individual auditory cortical regions to reconstructed audio representations.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Ciferri, Tonio Weidler, Matteo Ferrante, Nicola Toschi, Elia Formisano

item.title: KR A1: Design and Preliminary Evaluation of a Humanoid-Robot Interaction Prototype Integrating Personalized Voice Synthesis, Contextual Dialogue, and Emotion-Aware Response Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09900v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents the design and preliminary evaluation of KR A1, a humanoid-robot interaction prototype that integrates personalized voice synthesis, contextual dialogue processing, and emotion-aware response generation for potential mental-healthcare applications. The system architecture combines a locally hosted large language model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, served via Ollama) for natural-language understanding and response generation, OpenVoice v2 for zero-shot speaker-adaptive speech synthesis, and a two-tier emotion-processing pipeline comprising a keyword heuristic and LLM-based inference. Face recognition (InsightFace) and vector memory retrieval (FAISS with sentence-transformer embeddings) enable user-personalized interaction. The experimental evaluation reported here is limited to the voice-cloning component: cloned voices were evaluated against reference recordings using eight acoustic similarity measures - mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, pitch, spectral centroid, spectral contrast, spectral rolloff, zero-crossing rate, formants, and speaker-embedding cosine similarity - supplemented by a same-speaker versus cross-speaker baseline comparison. All tests were conducted on a small, informal development sample; no statistical significance testing against a held-out baseline was performed. The emotion-recognition accuracy, end-to-end response latency, and therapeutic or clinical impact of the integrated system have not yet been formally evaluated and are identified as directions for future work. All testing was informal and self-conducted by the development team; no patients or external human participants were involved, and the system has not been evaluated or deployed in a clinical setting.
item.dc:creator: Mahek Aanthu, Om Aanthu, Aaryan AK Aanthu

item.title: Industry case studies of adapting TTS for smooth interactions
item.description: arXiv:2611.09914v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern, neural-based ASR and TTS systems for speech communication are now very sophisticated, but they are frequently designed for average users in more idealized scenarios, which can underperform when interacting with users having specialized listening needs, or who speak in non-standard ways. Here we review recent TTS research, and note that industrial, production-level implementations of adaptive TTS systems are scarce. We describe how we implemented changes to TTS systems based on prior research, and then report qualitative results from two case studies, where adapted TTS techniques are applied to real-world HRI settings: First, in an older adult care home, and second, in an airport, where noise levels create comprehension problems. Results suggest promising directions using relatively simple modifications to pitch, duration, and intensity of the robot's speech, and offer a framework for larger, more formal studies of how TTS adaptations can improve HRI.
item.dc:creator: Paige Tutt\"osi, El\'eonore Ferrier-Barbut, Anais Scipioni, Olivia Yung, Ha Eun Shim, Ajla Basic, Yue Wang, H. Henny Yeung

item.title: Ninada: Sub-Clause Split-Graph VITS Streaming and Capability-Routed 24 kHz Speech Synthesis Across Twelve Scripts
item.description: arXiv:2611.10035v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: End-to-end VITS text-to-speech models synthesize natural speech in a single forward pass, yet standard ONNX exports execute monolithically over an entire clause, delaying Time-To-First-Audio (TTFA) to several seconds and spiking activation memory. Client-side deployment across Indic scripts faces four further bottlenecks: 138.8 MB float32 checkpoints per language strain browser caches, mobile WebGPU stalls for 6-14 s compiling convolution shaders while still running slower than real time ($1.44\times$ RTF), small WebAssembly pthread pools stall at barriers on big.LITTLE mobile CPUs, and mobile Web Audio pipelines drop frames or mute output under AudioWorklet contention and iOS WKWebView rules. We present Ninada, an open-source 24 kHz TTS system covering English, Classical Sanskrit, and ten Indian languages (sa, en, hi, kn, mr, bn, ta, te, ml, gu, pa, or) across a capability-routed 48-checkpoint fleet: 24 studio HiFi-GAN v1 specialists (27.9 MB W8A32+FP16 ONNX) for desktop/WebGPU and 24 distilled c8c8_384 iSTFTNet specialists (21.7 MB ONNX, $2.64\times$ fewer vocoder MACs via an exact NOLA dual-window ConvTranspose1d inverse STFT with zero complex ops) for mobile WASM, plus a 0.0 MB zero-dependency Klatt fallback. At runtime, Ninada splits a single ONNX file in memory in $< 15$ ms into prior, flow, and windowed vocoder sub-sessions streaming 12-frame halos with raised-cosine crossfades. On $N = 480$ held-out 24 kHz studio utterances, Ninada achieves 3.22 dB 0-8 kHz MCD (3.09 dB mobile iSTFTNet; 1.33 dB 24-voice distillation MCD, vs. 5.17 dB for the 1,526.8 MB 16 kHz Meta MMS fleet) and 6.07 dB 8-12 kHz error, delivering 89-155 ms audible startup on desktop WebGPU and 538-649 ms zero-underrun streaming at 0.75-0.76x RTF on a physical Google Pixel 10 Pro XL.
item.dc:creator: Hemanth HM

item.title: M5-TTS: A Mini-Scale Multilingual and Multi-Dialect Text-to-Speech Language Model with Multi-Token Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.10162v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present M5-TTS, a compact text-to-speech system supporting multilingual and Chinese multidialect synthesis, zero-shot voice cloning, speaker-specific multilingual generation, and CPU streaming. Its 50M-parameter language model, excluding the speech codec, combines a temporal backbone with a local multi-token prediction module over 16 codebooks. GRPO post-training combines global speaker-similarity and pause feedback with a token-level CER process advantage. Character-level error comparisons provide local feedback, with negative credit propagated backward within a clause and projected onto audio-token positions. M5-TTS achieves 1.37% CER on Seed-ZH and 2.91% WER on Seed-EN, corresponding to relative error reductions of 62.2% and 35.3% over MOSS-TTS-Nano with half the language-model parameters. It also achieves lower content error rates in five of six evaluated MiniMax languages, while difficult Chinese inputs remain a limitation. On four Intel Xeon Gold 6530 cores, it achieves a real-time factor of 0.653 and a warm first-chunk latency of 225ms. A 10-listener evaluation gives M5-TTS higher speaker-similarity and intelligibility ratings than MOSS-TTS-Nano, with a lower naturalness rating. We will release training, post-training, and inference code, together with voice-cloning and speaker-specific checkpoints, to support reproducible research on compact speech generation for on-device voice interaction.
item.dc:creator: Wenhao Li, Jingbin Hu, Shengming Ling, Xiaming Ren, Haoyu Zhang, Jinrui Liang, Hanke Xie, Qirui Zhan, Guobin Ma, Huakang Chen, Chunbo Hao, Jianguo Zheng, Wenkang Hou, Dake Guo, Yuepeng Jiang, Linhan Ma, Yunxiang Chen, Houdun Liu, Su Feng, Chuang Ding, Pengcheng Zhu, Liumeng Xue, Lei Xie

item.title: Lightweight Neural Prediction for MDCT-Based Perceptual Audio Coding
item.description: arXiv:2611.10192v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Perceptual audio codecs often use predictive coding to further reduce signal redundancy. Rather than learning the entire codec pipeline end-to-end, we insert a small neural network as a drop-in, deterministic predictor in an otherwise conventional codec: the network estimates the next Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT) coefficient block from a short context of reconstructed blocks, and the encoder transmits the quantized residual. We compare Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) predictors against a non-predictive baseline and a per-line Normalized Least Mean Squares (NLMS) linear predictor (similar to the MPEG-2 AAC Main Profile predictor). The CNN consistently outperforms the MLP, the linear predictor, and the baseline in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), noise-to-mask ratio (NMR), and MUSHRA evaluation scores. Using a 512-sample analysis window (w = 512), our neural predictors recover, and the CNN exceeds, the coded quality obtained by the non-predictive baseline after quadrupling the analysis-window length to w = 2048, at substantially lower algorithmic delay. The CNN uses only 0.13M parameters (roughly 20x fewer than the MLP) and has a decoder real-time factor (RTF) of ~0.10 on a consumer CPU.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proc. AES Show 2026 Nashville (161st AES Convention), Oct. 2026, Paper 50
item.dc:creator: Niccolo Abate, Gabriel Soule, Marina Bosi

item.title: Pandemonium: Longform Target-Speaker Speech Recognition with Cross-Speaker Interactions
item.description: arXiv:2611.10659v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diarization-conditioned target-speaker ASR (TS-ASR), in particular Diarization-conditioned Whisper (DiCoW), is an accurate and data-efficient approach to multi-talker transcription. It has, however, three structural limitations: the model transcribes each speaker independently, operates on short (30 s) windows, and optimizes its diarization and TS-ASR components separately. We address the first two. We integrate the diarization conditioning into a longform Parakeet backbone (DiCoP) and add cross-speaker attention, which lets the model attend across the speaker dimension so that speakers are no longer decoded in isolation, and an STNO mask refiner that re-estimates the diarization-derived conditioning. As conversational data with genuine multi-speaker interaction is scarce, we scale training with a pseudo-labeling pipeline that mines 5.4k hours of in-the-wild multi-speaker audio from YODAS2. Combining these with synthetic and real data yields state-of-the-art results across several meeting benchmarks. We open-source the resulting models, DiCoP and Pandemonium, and the pseudo-labeled data.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Polok, Dominik Klement, Ivan Medennikov, Antoine Laurent, Petr P\'alka, Samuele Cornell, Shinji Watanabe, Sanjeev Khudanpur, Jagadeesh Balam, Jan \v{C}ernock\'y, Luk\'a\v{s} Burget, Matthew Wiesner

item.title: LongCap: Hour-Scale Timestamped Audio Captioning via Chunk-wise Processing
item.description: arXiv:2611.11125v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Describing hours of audio requires accurate event timing and sustained descriptive detail throughout the recording. We present LongCap, a framework for timestamped audio captioning (TAC), with the human-annotated LongCapBench and three diarization-inspired metrics: Timeline Error Rate (TER), Granularity Error Rate (GER), and Caption Similarity (tcpCapSim). LongCap interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and retained context to support length extrapolation within a 1M-token inference context window. Event-level reannotation restores caption detail, while systematic studies examine model scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation. LongCap-Diar achieves strong benchmark results and extrapolates to 16 hours of concatenated audio despite training on recordings no longer than 40 minutes. Our TAC models are competitive with Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus on short clips, outperform evaluated baselines in caption similarity and timeline accuracy in segment-level comparisons on LongCapBench-TAC-Long, and caption full recordings approaching two hours. On LongCapBench-TAC, 9B and 35B-A3B offer favorable size-performance tradeoffs, while 122B-A10B substantially improves event-dependency recovery. These findings support long-horizon general audio understanding and provide a foundation for always-on voice agents.
item.dc:creator: Jinchuan Tian, Sen Chen, Wenbin Huang, Chao Weng, Zhengwei Huang, Jiatong Shi, Yichen Lu, Haoran Wang, Shinji Watanabe, Cong Zhou

item.title: CallCleaner: Lightweight Bioacoustic Denoising from an Audio Foundation Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.11491v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many studies of animal vocalizations require clean recordings, but animals are usually recorded in the field, with background noise from weather, vehicles, and other animals. Animal vocalization denoising is challenged by the scarcity of clean training data and the extreme diversity of animal vocalizations. Classical spectral gates leave residual noise, especially without voice activity detection (VAD), while detector-free neural denoisers designed for bioacoustics remove less noise. We show that a general-purpose source separation foundation model, SAM-Audio, removes more noise than either of these types of methods, when used without training and prompted with time spans from a simple animal VAD. To turn this heavy method into a practical tool, we distill it into CallCleaner, a 19M-parameter denoiser that needs no detector and runs ~90x faster than real time on a laptop CPU. We find that SI-SDR has limited utility in our setting as it penalizes regenerated output and conflates noise removal with call fidelity, a trade-off our separate metrics reveal. CallCleaner leaves 11 dB less noise around the call than Biodenoising, the leading neural bioacoustic denoiser with public weights, and among fast, CPU-capable systems it pushes the Pareto frontier of noise removal vs. call fidelity, without requiring a detector. We release code and weights for CallCleaner, which enables fast, private, local denoising of single-caller recordings without specialized hardware.
item.dc:creator: Michael Xie, Ga\v{s}per Begu\v{s}, Morris Alper

item.title: Discriminator-free adversarial domain adaptation for robust speech classification
item.description: arXiv:2611.12119v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The performance of speech classification systems such as speech emotion recognition or pathological speech detection can degrade substantially when there is a domain shift between training and test data. This shift can arise due to e.g., differences in recording setup, acoustic environment, speaker, language, or speaking style. Adversarial domain adaptation addresses this problem by encouraging representations that are less sensitive to domain-specific differences. However, many adversarial approaches rely on training a separate domain discriminator, which can be unstable and difficult to train. In this paper, we propose to use a discriminator-free adversarial learning network (DALN) for unsupervised domain adaptation in speech classification tasks. DALN reuses the task classifier as an implicit discriminator and aligns domains through the nuclear-norm Wasserstein discrepancy on classifier outputs. We extensively evaluate the performance of DALN on intra-lingual, cross-lingual, and noisy adaptations for speech emotion recognition and pathological speech detection. Extensive experimental results show that DALN generally achieves the best performance across the considered tasks and domain shifts, outperforming discriminator-based domain adaptation approaches.
item.dc:creator: Yacouba Kaloga, Ina Kodrasi

item.title: SCLAP: Temporal structural alignment improves localization in long-form audio
item.description: arXiv:2611.12124v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Audio-text models such as Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP) typically pool frame and token sequences uniformly into global embeddings. This discards temporal structure and impairs both retrieval and localization, especially for short events in long recordings. We introduce SCLAP, a sequence-level contrastive framework that aligns audio frames and text tokens using monotone one-dimensional optimal transport. Its learned marginals and transport plan provide fine-grained temporal supervision from clip-level captions alone. On short-form audio (i.e., Clotho and TACOS datasets with 15-30s recordings), SCLAP remains competitive for retrieval while improving zero-shot localization over CLAP and Text-aware Attention Pooling. On long-form audio (i.e., CASTELLA dataset with up to 300s recordings), SCLAP improves retrieval performance and its localization advantage grows as the event-to-context ratio decreases. At inference, SCLAP requires no optimal transport computation since retrieval can use pooled embeddings and localization can use inexpensive frame-text cosine scores.
item.dc:creator: Yacouba Kaloga, Ina Kodrasi

item.title: REAL: Reward Modeling through Evidence-Linked Analysis of Lifelikeness in Generated Speech
item.description: arXiv:2611.12406v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As modern text-to-speech systems become increasingly intelligible and natural, evaluation is shifting from detecting gross synthesis failures to identifying subtle departures from lifelike human delivery. Because large-scale listening tests are costly and slow, speech reward models can serve as scalable automatic judges for comparing generated utterances, curating data, and supporting iterative TTS development. Existing speech reward models can predict scores or pairwise preferences and may generate natural-language rationales, but their supervision is typically defined at the utterance or pair level. The connection between local acoustic phenomena and the final preference therefore remains implicit. We introduce REAL, a framework for Reward modeling through Evidence-linked Analysis of Lifelikeness in generated speech. Its central idea is to supervise not only the final pairwise preference but also a structured account of its supporting observations, linking local audio spans to perceptual phenomena, affected dimensions, and the overall judgment. Specifically, REAL-Jury constructs these evidence-linked reports through timestamp alignment, multi-model analysis, and dispute-oriented deliberation. REAL-Judge learns to generate them from paired audio inputs. REAL-Eval assesses preference prediction in two tiers, from salient perceptual differences to subtle distinctions among strong TTS systems. Instantiated with MiMo-Audio, REAL-Judge improves pairwise preference accuracy over its backbone by 16.01 and 11.41 percentage points on the two tiers, respectively, and outperforms the open-source speech reward models SpeechJudge and UniSRM on both tiers.
item.dc:creator: Yaodong Song, Jie Lian, Xusheng Yang, Genliang Zhao, Hongjie Chen, Jian Kang, Zhen-Hua Ling, Jie Li, Yongxiang Li

item.title: Can Large Language Models Aid in Annotating Speech Emotional Data? Uncovering New Frontiers
item.description: arXiv:2307.06090v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite recent advancements in speech emotion recognition (SER) models, state-of-the-art deep learning (DL) approaches face the challenge of the limited availability of annotated data. Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionised our understanding of natural language, introducing emergent properties that broaden comprehension in language, speech, and vision. This paper examines the potential of LLMs to annotate abundant speech data, aiming to enhance the state-of-the-art in SER. We evaluate this capability across various settings using publicly available speech emotion classification datasets. Leveraging ChatGPT, we experimentally demonstrate the promising role of LLMs in speech emotion data annotation. Our evaluation encompasses single-shot and few-shots scenarios, revealing performance variability in SER. Notably, we achieve improved results through data augmentation, incorporating ChatGPT-annotated samples into existing datasets. Our work uncovers new frontiers in speech emotion classification, highlighting the increasing significance of LLMs in this field moving forward.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: IEEE Computational Intelligence Magazine, vol. 20, no. 1, pp. 66-77, 2025
item.dc:creator: Siddique Latif, Muhammad Usama, Mohammad Ibrahim Malik, Bj\"orn W. Schuller

item.title: TsetlinKWS: A 65nm 16.58uW, 0.63mm2 State-Driven Convolutional Tsetlin Machine-Based Accelerator For Keyword Spotting
item.description: arXiv:2510.24282v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Tsetlin Machine (TM) has recently attracted attention as a low-power alternative to neural networks due to its simple and interpretable inference mechanisms. However, its performance on speech-related tasks remains limited. This paper proposes TsetlinKWS, the first algorithm-hardware co-design framework for the Convolutional Tsetlin Machine (CTM) on the 12-keyword spotting task. Firstly, we introduce a novel Mel-Frequency Spectral Coefficient and Spectral Flux (MFSC-SF) feature extraction scheme together with spectral convolution, achieving a record-high accuracy of 87.35% for TM-based models on the 12-keyword spotting task. Secondly, we develop an Optimized Grouped Block-Compressed Sparse Row (OG-BCSR) algorithm that delivers a remarkable 9.84$\times$ reduction in model size, significantly improving the storage efficiency of CTMs. Finally, we propose a state-driven architecture tailored for CTMs, which simultaneously exploits data reuse and sparsity to attain high energy efficiency. The full system is evaluated in 65 nm process technology, consuming 16.58 $\mu$W at 0.7 V with a compact 0.63 mm$^2$ core area. TsetlinKWS demonstrates a Power-Performance-Area (PPA) product of 60.2 and requires only 907k logic operations per inference, corresponding to 1.4$\times$ and 10$\times$ reductions, respectively, compared with state-of-the-art KWS accelerators. These results position the CTM as a highly efficient candidate for ultra-low-power speech applications.
item.dc:creator: Baizhou Lin, Yuetong Fang, Renjing Xu, Rishad Shafik, Jagmohan Chauhan

item.title: X-Talk: On the Underestimated Potential of Modular Speech-to-Speech Dialogue System
item.description: arXiv:2512.18706v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present X-Talk, an open-source framework that champions a decoupled, modular design for LLM-driven speech-to-speech (S2S) systems. While the dominant trend favors end-to-end (E2E) modeling to optimize information flow, these "omni-models" often struggle to balance the competing objectives of complex speech tasks within a single network. X-Talk challenges this paradigm by demonstrating that a systematically optimized cascaded pipeline can achieve sub-second latency without sacrificing modular flexibility. Our framework seamlessly integrates specialized front-end components (e.g., VAD, speech enhancement) and diverse understanding models (e.g., ASR, emotion, and environmental sound analysis) with LLM capabilities like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and tool use. By revitalizing the cascaded approach, X-Talk highlights the underestimated potential of modular S2S systems and provides a robust foundation for future research and applications.
item.dc:creator: Zhanxun Liu, Yifan Duan, Mengmeng Wang, Pengchao Feng, Haotian Zhang, Xiaoyu Xing, Yijia Shan, Haina Zhu, Yuxiang Zhao, Bei Liu, Yuhang Dai, Chaochao Lu, Xipeng Qiu, Lei Xie, Lan Wang, Nan Yan, Zilong Zheng, Ziyang Ma, Kai Yu, Xie Chen

item.title: The World is Not Mono: Enabling Spatial Understanding in Large Audio-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2601.02954v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large audio-language models have made rapid progress in recognizing what is present in an audio clip, but spatial audio-language understanding still lacks a clear task interface. A model must also decide where sound events occur, which semantic and spatial attributes belong to the same auditory object, how multiple objects are arranged, and whether a scene-level answer is physically plausible. We formalize this capability as audio scene analysis (ASA), a three-level problem spanning atomic perception, relational integration, and cognitive reasoning. We propose The World is Not Mono (TWNM), a framework that equips audio-language models with explicit spatial evidence. TWNM uses physically grounded First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) simulation for controllable supervision, learns slot-regularized spatial representations from multichannel audio, fuses them with semantic audio features, and trains with a progressive curriculum ending in preference optimization over metadata-derived correct answers and auxiliary format/evidence rewards. To operationalize ASA, we build a controlled benchmark from scene metadata, covering localization, attribute binding, spatial comparison, scene abduction, and counterfactual reasoning. On this benchmark, TWNM achieves 70.8% overall accuracy, 66.4% on spatial-family tasks, and 79.76% on mixed $\mathcal{L}_3$ scene-level QA under exact multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) scoring. We also audit monaural and binaural reference systems as diagnostic references with explicit audit labels, since they differ in spatial input, training interface, and output format. The supported claim is that a clearly defined ASA hierarchy, FOA-conditioned spatial representations, and metadata-grounded training enable controlled, auditable spatial audio-language reasoning, with STARSS23 providing a limited real-recording diagnostic.
item.dc:creator: Yuhuan You, Lai Wei, Tianshu Qu

item.title: Embryonic Exposure to VPA Influences Chick Vocalisations: A Computational Study
item.description: arXiv:2601.12203v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In young animals like poultry chicks (Gallus gallus), vocalisations convey information about affective and behavioural states. Traditional approaches to vocalisation analysis, relying on manual annotation and predefined categories, introduce biases, limit scalability, and fail to capture the full complexity of vocal repertoires. We introduce a computational framework for the automated detection, acoustic feature extraction, and unsupervised learning of chick vocalisations. Applying this framework to a dataset of newly hatched chicks, we identified two primary vocal clusters. We then tested our computational framework on an independent dataset of chicks exposed during embryonic development to vehicle or Valproic Acid (VPA), a compound that disrupts neural development and is linked to autistic-like symptoms. Clustering analysis on the experimental dataset confirmed two primary vocal clusters and revealed systematic differences between groups. VPA-exposed chicks showed an altered repertoire, with a relative increase in softer calls. VPA differentially affected call clusters, modulating temporal, frequency, and energy domain features. Overall, VPA-exposed chicks produced vocalisations with shorter duration, reduced pitch variability, and modified energy profiles, with the strongest alterations observed in louder calls. This study provides a computational framework for analysing chick vocalisations, advancing knowledge of early-life communication in typical and atypical vocal development.
item.dc:creator: Antonella M. C. Torrisi, In\^es Nolasco, Paola Sgad\`o, Elisabetta Versace, Emmanouil Benetos

item.title: Do Joint Audio-Video Generation Models Understand Physics?
item.description: arXiv:2605.07061v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Joint audio-video generation models are rapidly approaching professional production quality, raising a central question: do they understand audio-visual physics, or merely generate plausible sounds and frames that violate real-world consistency? We introduce AV-Phys Bench, a benchmark for evaluating physical commonsense in joint audio-video generation. AV-Phys Bench tests models across three scene categories: Steady State, Event Transition, and Environment Transition. It covers physics-grounded subcategories drawn from real-world scenes, plus Anti-AV-Physics prompts that deliberately request physically inconsistent audio-video behavior. Each generation is evaluated along five dimensions: visual semantic adherence, audio semantic adherence, visual physical commonsense, audio physical commonsense, and cross-modal physical commonsense. Across three proprietary and four open-source models, we find that Seedance 2.0 performs best overall, but all models remain far from robust physical understanding. Performance drops sharply on event-driven and environment-driven transitions, and even strong proprietary systems collapse on Anti-AV-Physics prompts. We further introduce AV-Phys Agent, a ReAct-style evaluator that combines a multimodal language model with deterministic acoustic measurement tools, producing rankings that closely align with human ratings. Our results identify cross-modal physical consistency and transition-driven scene dynamics as key open challenges for joint audio-video generation.
item.dc:creator: Zijun Cui, Xiulong Liu, Hao Fang, Mingwei Xu, Jiageng Liu, Zexin Xu, Weiguo Pian, Shijian Deng, Feiyu Du, Chenming Ge, Yapeng Tian

item.title: PitchBench: Measuring Pitch Hearing in Audio-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.26176v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) are increasingly used in real-world applications that require music understanding, including tutoring, captioning, recommendation, and production. Yet existing benchmarks rarely evaluate a fundamental component of this understanding: pitch hearing. Pitch underpins the identification of notes, chords, and melodies and the grounding of captions in musical events, but it remains unclear how reliably ALMs perceive fine-grained pitch across sound sources, acoustic conditions, and response formats. We introduce PitchBench, an evaluation suite comprising 28 tasks that assess absolute and relative pitch perception under variations in loudness, note duration, sound source, time stretching, background noise, and other acoustic conditions. Tasks range from identifying isolated pitches to tracking voices in four-part musical textures. Evaluating frontier ALMs, we find that pitch hearing remains highly unreliable. Models perform poorly across settings, with accuracy varying sharply depending on the notation or prompt format, indicating instruction drift. Specialized DSP and neural pitch baselines achieve mean scores of approximately 73.2% and 75.2%, respectively, compared with approximately 53.9% for the strongest ALM. We release PitchBench as an evaluation benchmark, a training dataset, and a Python package with data generation tools to support future research on pitch-aware audio-language modeling.
item.dc:creator: Milan Liessens Dujardin, Song-Ze Yu, Craver Corbyn Thomas-Smith, David M. Chan, Karina Nguyen

item.title: VocalCoachBench: Benchmarking Audio-Language Models on Expert Feedback for Singing
item.description: arXiv:2609.04241v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent audio-language models are increasingly evaluated on recognizing, describing, and reasoning about audio, but expert-facing applications require a different capability: producing feedback that identifies problems and suggests corrective actions grounded in the input. We introduce VocalCoachBench, a benchmark for evaluating audio-language models on expert vocal coaching feedback for singing. VocalCoachBench contains 515 recordings annotated by 18 professional vocal trainers, yielding 1,064 expert audio-level reviews and 12,216 atomic coaching claims. It comprises a same-song subset for controlled comparison and a diverse-song subset for segment-grounded feedback across varied songs and recording conditions. To accommodate the open-ended nature of expert feedback, VocalCoachBench separates deterministic structured targets from claim-based assessment of free-form diagnosis and corrective guidance. Human annotation analysis shows that expert agreement varies strongly with label granularity, motivating hierarchical structured metrics and claim-based evaluation of open-ended feedback. Experiments with 12 recent audio-language models reveal a persistent gap: while the strongest models can compare performances and identify broad issue domains in free-form feedback, the best Top-3 macro-F1 only slightly exceeds a label-prior baseline, and strict diagnosis hit rates remain below 8%. To our knowledge, VocalCoachBench provides the first public testbed for evaluating audio-grounded expert feedback for singing, moving audio-language evaluation beyond description toward analytic feedback. Data, code, and audio examples are available at https://hayeonbang.github.io/VocalCoachBench.
item.dc:creator: Hayeon Bang, Hounsu Kim, Wonil Kim, Juhan Nam

item.title: Leakage-aware acoustic drone detection: fusing hand-crafted and pretrained audio features in a stacking ensemble
item.description: arXiv:2611.04714v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Small multirotor drones produce a characteristic acoustic signature, and microphones offer a low-cost way to detect them. High accuracies have been reported on public drone audio benchmarks, often with random clip-level splits of datasets built from a few long recordings and pieces of existing sound collections, so pieces of one source can appear in both training and test data. We study the binary task of the public DroneAudioDataset (11,704 one-second clips). Its 1,332 drone clips come from 257 five-second chunks of 7 recordings, and 96.4% of its non-drone clips are pieces of the 2,000 clips of the ESC-50 sound dataset. A grouped, source-disjoint protocol (five folds, three repeats) is compared with a random split. Each clip is described by 57 hand-crafted acoustic descriptors, reduced by a hybrid minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance and ReliefF selection or by NSGA-II multi-objective search, and by a 1024-dimensional embedding from the pretrained YAMNet network. Random Forest and XGBoost learners on both views form a stacking ensemble. Under the grouped protocol, the two-view stack reached a mean accuracy of 95.29% (SD 1.62 points over 15 test folds), a specificity of 98.29% and an area under the ROC curve of 0.990, and it correctly classified 98.78% of unseen ESC-50 source clips as non-drone. The random split overstated accuracy by 1.89 to 3.22 points for the four models. Adding YAMNet embeddings to the hand-crafted view raised accuracy by 1.11 points (higher in 12 of 15 folds). Hybrid selection matched the accuracy of all 44 baseline descriptors with 16 to 18 features, and NSGA-II retained 4 to 6 features at lower accuracy. The stack took 51.0 ms per clip on one CPU thread. Source-disjoint evaluation exposes the optimism of random splits and gives a reliable benchmark, and fusing hand-crafted with YAMNet features consistently improves detection in real time on one CPU thread.
item.dc:creator: Zahid Iqbal

item.title: EvolveCaptions: Empowering DHH Users Through Real-Time Collaborative Captioning
item.description: arXiv:2510.02181v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems often struggle to accurately transcribe speech from Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DHH) speakers. Existing personalization approaches typically require substantial pre-recorded datasets and burden DHH users. We present EvolveCaptions, a collaborative, error-driven personalization system that connects caption correction with speaker-specific ASR adaptation. When transcribing a DHH speaker's speech, hearing partners repair transcription errors, and the system generates short, targeted clauses for the DHH speaker to record. These samples are used to incrementally fine-tune the model. In a study with 12 DHH and six hearing participants, EvolveCaptions reduced Word Error Rate (WER) across five scripted reading rounds, requiring an average of five minutes of additional speech recording. Participants found the interfaces usable but considered recording and correction effortful; acceptability depended on context and anticipated long-term benefit. These findings show the potential of collaborative, cumulative adaptation while exposing the labor and conditions needed to sustain it.
item.dc:creator: Liang-Yuan Wu, Dhruv Jain

item.title: MINT-Bench: A Comprehensive Multilingual Benchmark for Instruction-Following Text-to-Speech
item.description: arXiv:2604.17958v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (TTS) has emerged as an important capability for controllable and expressive speech generation, yet its evaluation remains underdeveloped due to limited benchmark coverage, weak diagnostic granularity, and insufficient multilingual support. We present \textbf{MINT-Bench}, a comprehensive multilingual benchmark for instruction-following TTS. MINT-Bench is built upon a hierarchical multi-axis taxonomy, a scalable multi-stage data construction pipeline, and a hierarchical hybrid evaluation protocol that jointly assesses content consistency, instruction following, and perceptual quality. Experiments across ten languages show that current systems remain far from solved: frontier commercial systems lead overall, while leading open-source models become highly competitive and can even outperform commercial counterparts in localized settings such as Chinese. The benchmark further reveals that harder compositional and paralinguistic controls remain major bottlenecks for current systems. We release MINT-Bench together with the data construction and evaluation toolkit to support future research on controllable, multilingual, and diagnostically grounded TTS evaluation. The leaderboard and demo are available at https://aslp-lab.github.io/MINT-Bench-Demo/

item.title: MuSP-Bench: Advanced Multimodal Benchmarking of Music Understanding across Score and Performance
item.description: arXiv:2608.28212v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Musicians commonly communicate musical intent through scores and performances. To investigate whether models can reason across both modalities, we introduce MuSP-Bench, a human-authored benchmark of 490 questions assessing understanding across Musical Scores and Performances, both individually and in combination. The benchmark spans interpretive and long-horizon reasoning across classical piano and orchestral works, represented through ABC notation, score images, MIDI, and audio. Our evaluation of frontier multimodal large language models reveals substantial difficulties in understanding musical scores and even greater challenges in reasoning about audio.
item.dc:creator: Milan Liessens Dujardin, Song-Ze Yu, Kevin Miao

item.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations
item.description: arXiv:2610.37364v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research.
